full_judgment:
2. In WP No. 4116 of 2007 the petitioner on behalf of the Waqf Administrator challenges the order of acquisition of the schedule property by the impugned gazette dated 07-9-2006 by which the property of the Waqf was included in acquisition. A subsequent application was made challenging the acquisition under LA Case No.138/61-62 on the ground that at the relevant time, in the year 1961-62, provisions of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 (TI Act, 1953) were not in existence. That application having been allowed, an additional prayer was inserted as A(1) "to show cause as to why the proceedings of LA Case No. 138/61-62 so far as it relates to the petitioner's land should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect." The petitioners have filed numerous affidavits and supplementary affidavits. The sum and substance of these is to the effect that the property belonged to a Waqf Estate, which was created in 1864 and 1877 and, therefore, it could not be the subject matter of acquisition. Moreover, it is claimed that the legal notices issued under the provisions for acquisition were not properly served upon either the Waqf Administrator or the petitioners. It is a further claim of the petitioners in their additional ground taken that section 93A of the TI Act of 1953 was inserted by Ordinance No.LXIX of 1958. The said ordinance of 1958 was repealed by Ordinance No.XXXVII of 1960 and, therefore, after the year 1960 section 93A did not exist in the statute books and any proceeding for acquisition under such law which did not exist has no legal basis. It is further claimed that although apparently in 1963 there was substitution of section 93A by Ordinance No.VI of 1963 that in effect is illegal since there cannot be any substitution of any provisions of law which did not at all exist at the relevant time. 

 5. The claim of the petitioners in both cases is that the land in question belonged to the Ainuddin and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate which was created in the year 1864 and 1877. After 1950, when the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into being, the property was taken over by the government and that was challenged in the civil court. The suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs claiming the land of the Waqf Estate. The matter went on appeal to the High Court and, thereafter, to the Supreme Court of Pakistan where the plaintiff's claim was established. Before us, initially the respondents claimed that the Waqf deed itself was a forgery and sought to produce a certified copy of another deed No.30 for the year 1864. However, in due course, the learned Deputy Attorney General having produced a number of original volumes for the year 1864, which were in the keeping of the District Registry, it became clear that deed No.30 dated 22.04.1864 is indeed a Waqf deed written in Persian and appears at pages 63-67 of Volume No.1 of 1864. The deed is contained within the volume which records Wills and the particular deed No.30 is a deed of Wakfnamah dated 22.04.1864 which was registered on 25.04.1864. In our mind there is no longer any doubt as to the authenticity of the said Waqf deed. 

 6. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the land belongs to the Waqf Estate and there is no longer in any doubt about that. Equally there is no doubt that no notice of the acquisition was issued either to the Waqf Administrator or to the present petitioners. He submits further that the acquisition process having commenced in the year 1961-62 under section 93A of the TI Act 1953, was done illegally, since between the years 1960 and 1963 there was no existence of section 93A of the TI Act, 1953 in the statute books and, therefore, any subsequent process of acquisition under this law which no longer existed at the time of the initiation of the LA case cannot be said to be legal. He further submits that in the year 1963 by Ordinance No. VI of 1963 section 93A was apparently substituted for the earlier section 93A(1). However, the learned advocate submits, this is also not legally correct since the substitution could only take place of an existing law and since the Ordinance o. LXIX of 1958, by which the section 93A had been introduced, was itself wholly repealed, there cannot arise any question or substitution. He submits that, therefore, the apparent existence of section 93A after 1963 is illegal and any subsequent proceeding is, therefore, illegal. 

 7. Mr. Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent-Government, submits that the properly in question was acquired properly under the provisions of section 93A of the TI Act 1953. He points out that although the acquisition was initiated in the year 1961-62 the process was suspended until alter the reintroduction of section 93A by Ordinance No.VI of 1963 and further notice was issued in 1965. He submits that since the law existed after 1963 there can be no question as to the legality or the procedure followed thereafter. The learned DAG further submits that the property described in the schedule is not part of the Waqf Estate since the schedule of the Waqf deed does not correspond ill any way to the schedule mentioned by the petitioners in their writ petitions. He submits that whether or not the property in question claimed by the petitioners is in fact part of the Waqf Estate is a disputed question of fact, which can only be ascertained after taking proper evidence in the civil court. The learned DAG also questions the maintainability or the writ petition in view of the fact that the petitioner in WP No. 4116 of 2007 is a person who is representing an association and did not file the writ petition in his personal capacity. 

 10. The substantive legal point raised by the petitioners is that the provision of law namely section 93A of the TI Act, 1953, under which the acquisition process took place, did not exist after 1960 when the Ordinance No. LXIX of 1958, by which section 93A had been introduced into the statute books, had been totally repealed. 

 11. We find from the relevant ordinances that the TI Act 1953 did not originally contain the provision of section 93A. The section was subsequently inserted, by Ordinance No. LXIX of 1958, for the purpose of requisition of property for any scheme. The section gives details of the procedure to be followed in case of requisition of property for a scheme and how the possession is to be taken and compensation to be paid. In the year 1960 by Amendment Ordinance No.XXXVII, the Ordinance No.LXIX of 1958 was totally repealed thereby deleting section 93A from the statute books. There is, therefore, substance in the argument of the learned advocate Mr.Nurul Amin that from the year 1960 section 93A no longer existed. On the other hand the claim of the respondents is that in the year 1963 by Amendment Ordinance No.VI of 1963, section 93A was reintroduced. Section 26 of the Town Improvement (Amendment) Ordinance, 1963 (Ordinance No.VI of 1963) provides as follows: 

 "( I) When any immovable property is required by the Board for carrying out any of the purposes of this Act, the Provincial Government may direct the Deputy Commissioner to requisition such property for the Board by an order in writing: 

 (ii) in sub-section (3), for the words "the Provincial Government may direct the District Magistrate to", the words "the Deputy Commissioner shall" shall be substituted; 

 "(a) The Provincial Government may, if it thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property for the Board, and shall, if it proposes to so acquire a requisitioned property, direct the Deputy Commissioner to cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property proposed to be acquired stating that the property is proposed to be acquired for the Board."; 

 13. The Ordinances have been placed before us, We find in the TI Act, 1953 (East Bengal Act. XIII of 1953) as modified up to 31.03.1967 (printed and issued from the Government Press) shows the existence of section 93A and it also appears from the footnotes that section 93A was inserted by the Town Improvement (Amendment) Ordinance 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance, LXIX of 1958, section 15) and note 2 shows that sub-section (1) of section 93A was substituted for the former sub-section by East Pakistan Ordinance, VI of 1963, section 26. It cannot be said, therefore, that this law was not in existence. We find that the law was very much in existence. Whether or not the word substituted was wrongly used and whether or not the use of the word "substituted" makes the law itself illegal is a matter which is not agitated before us, inasmuch as the vires of law by which section 93A was "substituted" or reintroduced in 1963 has not been challenged. Moreover, even if the law has been wrongly reintroduced into the statute books, it cannot be said that all transactions thereafter are to be negated by the fact that the introduction of the law was illegal. We have to bear in mind also that had the word substituted not been used and the provision simply inserted into the statue books, there could not have been any such arguments as are placed before us now. Moreover.the law came into being, rightly or wrongly, in the year 1963 and no challenge has been made against it until now. Had the law been challenged at the appropriate time, then the authority concerned may have simply inserted the very same provision in the law without calling it a 'substitution' or they may have had recourse to other methods of acquisition. There is no dearth of law to allow acquisition by the government or other authority needing property for the public interest. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 as well as the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 were very much in existence and could have been used following the procedures in those laws. We find; therefore, that the provisions of law which have been followed cannot now be challenged by the petitioners who are standing in the shoes of the original owners, who apparently did not challenge the propriety of the law itself. We may mention here that section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 was finally repealed by section 23 of the Town Improvement (Amendment) Act, 1987.
